analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top capital gains tax rate to 14% for individuals and 28% for corporations, and adjusts asset values for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the maximum tax rate on capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets — from 28% to 14% for individuals (and 7.5% for those in the lowest bracket), and set a 28% capital gains rate for corporations, down from the top 35% corporate rate. It also would have increased the value of assets held more than three years for tax purposes to account for inflation, reducing taxable gains. It was introduced on the first day of the 105th Congress with 159 cosponsors, but the House tax-writing committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations that realize capital gains — mainly shareholders, business sellers, and owners of appreciated property. Capital gains are concentrated among wealthier households, so the largest dollar benefits would flow to high-income filers. Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts also receive special pass-through indexing rules in the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the individual capital gains rate at 14%, with a 7.5% rate for gains falling within the 15% income bracket, replacing the prior 20%/10% maximum rates.
Sets a 28% alternative capital gains rate for corporations in place of the up-to-35% regular corporate rate, applying to capital gains for corporations, and conforming rules for foreign withholding.

Indexes the basis of assets — corporate stock and tangible property held more than three years — for inflation using the GDP deflator, so gains attributable purely to rising prices would not be taxed.

Extends the indexing adjustment through partnerships, S corporations, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and common trust funds, with special rules to pass the benefit to investors in those vehicles.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the revenue cost of lower rates and inflation adjustments, since the bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions; the cost ultimately falls on other taxpayers or adds to the deficit. Taxpayers whose gains come from wages-based savings rather than appreciated assets get no comparable benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers overall and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: The rate cuts and inflation indexing are not offset by any revenue-raising provisions in the bill, so their full cost to the Treasury would add to deficits or require cuts or tax increases elsewhere.

The indexing benefit applies only to assets held more than three years and excludes depreciation-related deductions, complicating the tax code and limiting the benefit to long-term holders of stock and tangible property.
The bill repeals the existing 50% exclusion for gain on certain small-business stock, trading one tax preference for another and changing treatment that small-business investors previously relied on.
Capital gains are realized overwhelmingly by higher-income households, so the largest benefits would accrue to the wealthiest taxpayers rather than to ordinary wage earners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully lower the cost of selling appreciated assets, which affects some middle-income households selling homes or small businesses, but its largest dollar benefits would flow to the top of the income distribution, where capital gains are concentrated. Because it includes no revenue offsets, the cost of the rate cuts and indexing would be borne broadly by other taxpayers or future budgets. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this is a targeted tax cut for asset holders, not a broad-based tax reduction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House tax-writing committee on the day it was introduced, its sponsor gave a series of floor speeches promoting it through July 1997, and it died there without ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Dreier introduced H.R. 14 on January 7, 1997, the first day of the 105th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill gathered 159 cosponsors — 140 Republicans and 19 Democrats — including original cosponsors from both parties.
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks on the measure repeatedly between January and July 1997, but no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.
No further action appears in the record after July 22, 1997, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers as a whole are better off because the bill died, since its rate cuts and inflation indexing carried no revenue offsets; the proposal's intended beneficiaries — holders of large capital gains — gained nothing from it in this form. Congress did separately enact a smaller capital gains rate cut later in 1997, but that was a different bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; large asset holders gained nothing

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and delivered repeated floor remarks promoting it from January through July 1997.

for.name: 19 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including two original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 7, 1997, and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: House Democratic leaders of the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Opposed deep capital gains rate cuts during the 1997 tax debate, backing a smaller cut than this bill proposed.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican — 140 Republicans versus 19 Democrats out of 159 total — and no vote ever occurred to test broader support.

industries.industry: Shareholders and sellers of appreciated assets
industries.note: The bill cuts their tax rate on investment profits to 14% and removes inflation-driven gains from taxation. Because capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, the gain would come at the cost of federal revenue that other taxpayers would otherwise share in.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill writes detailed rules letting these investment vehicles pass inflation-indexing benefits through to their investors, formalizing their role as the channel for the indexing benefit. Fund shareholders receive part of the benefit, but the rules are built around the funds' existing position.
A 28% maximum rate on corporate capital gains, down from the top 35% regular corporate rate, reduces the tax on corporate asset sales. The forgone revenue is borne broadly by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Small-business owners holding qualified small business stock
industries.note: The bill repeals the 50% exclusion for gain on certain small-business stock but replaces it with a flat 14% rate on all gains, so some holders do better and some worse depending on their situation.
